video_title: Scott Bessent Just Tied the Fed's Hands
gist: Danny Moses argues the Treasury's expanded long-bond buyback - roughly $128bn a year, only 2.4% of outstanding debt and funded with T-bill issuance - is pure messaging that has already round-tripped in yields and dollar-yen, while mechanically making it impossible for Fed chair Warsh to raise rates in September. The pair see the real September event as an 86%-probability Bank of Japan hike, treat a hawkish Warsh at Jackson Hole as an intraday buy-the-dip trade, and flag GPU-backed data-center securitization, Walmart's price-cut-driven comp miss, and Carvana's above-market loan sales as where the debt-and-funding strain surfaces in single names.

themes.theme: Treasury Buybacks Box In the Fed

insights.claim: The Treasury's expanded long-bond buyback (from $2bn to at least $4bn per operation) would repurchase roughly $128bn of 10-to-30-year paper over a year, which is only about 2.4% of outstanding debt and roughly 30% of expected issuance, so it is a signaling exercise rather than genuine curve control.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Fade the idea that buybacks can cap long yields; size the program against issuance before pricing any durable term-premium relief.
insights.quote: That is only 2.4% of the outstanding debt. It might be 30% of what they're expected to issue.

insights.claim: Funding long-dated Treasury buybacks by issuing T-bills mechanically removes the Fed's ability to raise rates, because a hike would blow up the cost of the bill issuance financing the operation.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Treasury debt management, not the Fed, is now setting the policy constraint - trade the front end as pinned regardless of inflation data.
insights.quote: You cannot raise rates. You cannot [laughter] raise rates in that situation.

insights.claim: The incoming Fed chair Warsh has effectively been sidelined by the Treasury before his first Jackson Hole, leaving him without the independence to tighten.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Positioning for a hawkish Fed pivot under Warsh is likely a losing trade; the constraint is fiscal, not preference.
insights.quote: I think Warsh is the lion who has no courage now. He can't do anything.

insights.claim: The market fully round-tripped the intervention within a day: the 30-year fell about nine basis points from 5.3% and the 10-year about eight or nine from roughly 4.72%, and both were back up five basis points by the next session while equities sold off further.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: The half-life of verbal/technical intervention is now under 48 hours - use rallies in long bonds after announcements as exit liquidity.

insights.claim: Dollar-yen has crept back toward 160 after the joint intervention a couple of weeks earlier pushed it below 158, showing the FX intervention is also failing to hold.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Watch 160 dollar-yen as the trigger level for the next round of intervention and for global risk-asset stress.

insights.claim: The announced Treasury buyback operations run only through November 4th, which lands on election timing and reinforces that the program is political messaging rather than a funding strategy.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Expect the program to be extended or escalated around the election rather than allowed to lapse quietly.

insights.claim: Bessent is a poor communicator whose condescending delivery is undermining the confidence-building job that is the entire point of the intervention.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If jawboning is the only real tool left, a messenger the market discounts means each intervention buys less time than the last.
insights.quote: he's one of the worst messengers, in my opinion

themes.theme: Debt, Dollar and the Stagflation Trap

insights.claim: With debt just past $40 trillion, a 6-7% deficit and rising inflation, long-end yields are backing up for structural funding reasons rather than technical ones, meaning real rates are heading higher because of the ability to fund the US, not because of growth.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Model equity risk premia off a rising real-rate floor; the bond selloff is a solvency signal, not a growth signal.

insights.claim: The only exit from the debt load is a weaker dollar, but weakening the dollar directly increases inflation pressure, which is the trap that has no policy off-ramp and is why gold keeps having its moment.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Own the debasement hedge: gold works in both branches of the fork, which is why the bid persists through rate backups.
insights.quote: you got to weaken the dollar. Well, if you weaken the dollar, you're just increasing inflation pressures

insights.claim: The US dollar is down to 58% of total currency circulating globally, and Fitch's reaffirmation of the AA+ rating cited reserve-currency status as the one positive against roughly a hundred negatives.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: The single pillar holding the US rating is eroding on a measurable trend line - a live input to the long-gold, short-dollar thesis.
insights.quote: no one's going to dare downgrade the US

insights.claim: Japan is currently a seller of US Treasuries, and the global debt problem is simultaneous rather than country-specific, which is what makes this cycle different from prior stress episodes.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: There is no marginal foreign buyer of last resort for the long end; watch Japanese repatriation flows as a driver of US term premium.

insights.claim: Treasuries are being crowded out by heavy corporate issuance, and at a full percentage point of extra yield a double-A or single-A corporate is now the preferred holding over government paper on a relative basis.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Relative-value case for high-grade corporates over Treasuries, with the caveat that if Treasuries fail nothing else is safe either.
insights.quote: Treasuries are competing with so much other issuance that's out there frankly from corporates other than Oracle that I would rather own

insights.claim: The 2008 crisis was never actually paid for; risk and debt were transferred from private to public balance sheets, and the global central bank experiment that began in Japan in 2001 is now coming home to roost.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Frames sovereign stress as the delayed bill for 2008 - argues against treating any single central bank action as a durable fix.

insights.claim: The path of least resistance is the 30-year making new highs back toward 5.35% and the 10-year to 4.75% alongside WTI moving from about $87.50 to the low $90s, which would force another policy climb-down - but each successive reversal is having less market impact because counterparties like China, Iran and Russia no longer fear it.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Concrete yield and oil levels to watch as the trigger for the next policy reversal, plus a reason to fade the reflex rally that follows it.

insights.claim: Companies setting 2027 budgets now face high energy input costs and higher borrowing needs simultaneously, which will make them ratchet back spending and turn stagflation from a slogan into a real earnings problem.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Watch 2027 guidance and capex commentary this fall as the first hard evidence of stagflationary retrenchment.

insights.claim: The administration cannot credibly promise deficit reduction because it just cut taxes, and a falling stock market would cut high-end tax receipts, so supporting equities has become a fiscal necessity rather than a preference.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Explains the persistent policy put under equities - and why talk of cutting capital gains taxes resurfaces whenever the tape weakens.

themes.theme: Jackson Hole and the September BOJ Trade

insights.claim: The CME FedWatch tool shows roughly 35% odds of a September hike, but both speakers put the true probability at zero for the September 16th meeting.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A 35% market-implied probability against a zero-conviction call is a direct mispricing to sell in front-end rates.

insights.claim: Bank of Japan hike odds for September 17th have gone from 25% three weeks ago to 86%, consistent with a quid pro quo in which the Treasury's yen support was traded for a Japanese hike, letting the yen strengthen without the Fed moving.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: The BOJ, not the Fed, is the September policy event for global carry - position yen and JGB-sensitive trades around the 17th.
insights.quote: Bessen told Japan, "You are raising rates. I'm doing this thing for you, you're going to do that for me."

insights.claim: If Warsh delivers a hawkish tone at Jackson Hole, the resulting equity selloff should be bought aggressively because the hawkishness cannot be backed by action and will be short-lived.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: A defined, dated, intraday trade setup around Friday's Jackson Hole speech.
insights.quote: It will be a massive trading opportunity to buy stocks just for, you know, maybe intraday if Warsh puts on a hawkish face at Jackson Hole on Friday, forget it. Buy everything you can

insights.claim: This year's Jackson Hole theme is financial innovation and its implications for payments and policy, which sits directly alongside the new data-center securitization market being built.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Any official commentary on securitized private-credit structures at Jackson Hole is a read-through for the AI financing complex.

themes.theme: AI Circular Financing and the Nvidia Print

insights.claim: The new data-center financing facility with Apollo, Blackstone, KKR and Goldman Sachs exists to keep the AI buildout going without using balance sheets, and was a response to widening CDS and credit spreads on AI-complex debt telling borrowers the capital markets were tightening.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Track AI-complex CDS and spreads as the leading indicator of capex capacity - the securitization is a symptom of stress, not strength.

insights.claim: BlackRock's Larry Fink compared the data-center securitization structure to the birth of mortgage-backed securities in the 1980s, an analogy that should be read as a warning rather than an endorsement.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: The sponsors themselves are naming the precedent - size exposure to GPU-backed paper accordingly.
insights.quote: I haven't seen financial innovation like this since mortgage-backed securities in the '80s. Fantastic, let's do it." That ended well.

insights.claim: Nvidia taking a 25% first-loss position on GPU-collateralized securitizations is economically equivalent to cutting chip prices 25%, which makes the facility look defensive rather than offensive.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: If the vendor is effectively subsidizing a quarter of the sale, reported economics on the AI revenue line overstate underlying demand.
insights.quote: why don't they just cut their chip prices by 25%?

insights.claim: Every partner in the AI financing structure has a vested interest in it succeeding - Brookfield wants power plants built, Goldman wants fees, Blackstone and BlackRock hold private-credit portfolios stuffed with these assets - which makes the structure self-reinforcing on the way up and highly correlated on the way down.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Treat AI data-center exposure as one correlated position across chips, private credit, power and alternative managers, not as diversified bets.

insights.claim: Turning AI data-center lending into a securitized asset class is what makes a future government bailout mechanically possible along TALF lines, because the government can buy a standardized asset class in a way it cannot buy bilateral loans.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Securitization is the pre-condition for socializing AI credit losses - a reason the structure will keep growing even if credit quality deteriorates.
insights.quote: He goes, "They'll figure it out." Guess what? Do you guys remember TALF?

insights.claim: The current AI vendor-financing web dwarfs the Lucent and Nortel circular-financing episode in complexity, which is why the Nvidia print matters more as an information source than as a trade.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Read the quarter for financing and circularity disclosures rather than for the headline beat, which is presumed.
insights.quote: It makes Lucent and Nortel circular thing look like a a you know, elementary school science project

insights.claim: Options are pricing only a 5% implied move for Nvidia's Wednesday report, about $15 on a $215 stock, which is unusually complacent for the single point of failure in the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Cheap optionality into a binary event for the market's most systemically important name.
insights.quote: it's a 5% implied move in the other direction, and really that's like 15 bucks on a $215 stock

insights.claim: Competition from Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs (including Google's chip work with Marvell), AMD, and Chinese buyers willing to take H100-class parts means there will eventually be a quarter where Nvidia's dominance cracks, even if this is not the quarter to be short it.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Neither long nor short into the print; the durable trade is in the custom-silicon supply chain rather than the incumbent.

insights.claim: Six DeepSeek-style efficiency shocks are likely within the next two quarters, which combined with any slowdown in the ability to fund AI growth would change the entire market narrative.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Cheap-model shocks and financing stress are the two tail risks to AI capex; either would hit the most crowded part of the index.
insights.quote: we have six deep seek moments here in the next, you know, two quarters, which I think are going to happen

insights.claim: Higher yields are specifically damaging to the AI complex because these are long-duration assets whose owners must keep raising debt after already using their balance sheets and cash flow.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: The bond market is the transmission channel to the AI trade - watch the long end as the risk gauge for megacap tech.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 looks headed back toward 7,500, with the rising 200-day moving average near roughly 7,100 - also the April breakout level - implying an easy 5-7% drawdown from recent highs heading into the midterms.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Defined downside targets and a technical support zone for sizing hedges into the fall.

insights.claim: With only about 5% of S&P 500 earnings left to report, conditions remain fairly constructive on earnings growth, and the bear case requires a pullback in R&D and capex plus higher unemployment rather than a valuation event alone.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Gives the specific conditions that would convert a technical drawdown into a real bear market - capex and labor, not multiples.

insights.claim: Crossing $40 trillion in debt made headlines for about seven minutes, but the current volume of deficit rhetoric is the highest in memory and is likely to stick now that investors see through the Treasury's attempt to lower borrowing costs.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Fiscal risk is becoming a persistent narrative rather than a one-day headline, which supports higher term premium and gold.
insights.quote: he just flopped, again use a poker reference, 2-7 offsuit

insights.claim: There is a bull market outside the index obsession - Latin America and Argentina, LNG, US MLPs, pipelines and infrastructure - and a weakening dollar would be a major positive for emerging markets, with single-stock hunting outside the indices now a lost art.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: A concrete rotation list for capital fleeing crowded AI exposure, leveraged to the same dollar-weakening thesis.
insights.quote: there's a bull market somewhere

insights.claim: Walmart beat on revenue and earnings but missed on same-store sales because it had to cut prices on items like beef to keep customers buying, and the stock fell 10% - the second straight quarter of a large post-earnings decline after a 9% drop last quarter.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Margin-funded traffic is the tell: the miss is on price realization, not demand, which is the classic late-cycle retail signal.

insights.claim: Walmart trades at roughly 35 times this year's earnings and 31.5 times next year's on high-single-digit earnings growth and mid-single-digit sales growth, putting it in the same de-rating category as Apple near 40 times - a premium multiple with no meme-able narrative to support it.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Multiple compression, not fundamentals, is the risk in defensive megacaps that got rerated on an AI-productivity story.

insights.claim: The US savings rate is the lowest in decades and gasoline and oil are staying bid, which hits Walmart's core customer directly and means the market is projecting the low-end consumer getting worse from here.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: The trade-down thesis is exhausting itself - watch consumer discretionary and the low end, which the market ignored while the high-end consumer absorbed the pressure.
insights.quote: the savings rate is the lowest it's been in decades for the consumer

insights.claim: At $103 Walmart looks likely to retest the November lows just below $100 and possibly the 52-week low near $95, because it remains a crowded trade that kept sliding for days after its last print.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Specific downside levels for a name still held as a defensive core position by many funds.

insights.claim: Carvana has been selling originated auto loans at prices of 109 to 111 when the going market rate for comparable paper is 103 to 104, and speculation points to insurance entities controlled by Guggenheim founder and Carvana shareholder Mark Walter - such as Delaware Life - as the buyer.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: If the premium gain-on-sale normalizes toward market pricing, Carvana earnings take a massive hit even though the arrangement may be entirely legal.
insights.quote: When the going rate in the market for those type of loans is 103 or 104

insights.claim: The Carvana situation grew out of a broader investigation into how insurance companies are being used inside private credit, making it a template for how affiliated insurance balance sheets can inflate reported economics elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Danny Moses (guest)
insights.so_what: Screen for other issuers whose gain-on-sale margins depend on a related-party insurance buyer.

insights.claim: Salesforce has rallied 40% off its recent lows but is still down 45% from its highs after being down 70%, and investors have refused to buy the AI strategy Benioff has been selling for two years, making this print the test of whether that changes.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: A heavily de-rated AI-narrative name where any credible monetization evidence has outsized upside given positioning.
insights.quote: Investors haven't been buying what Mark Benioff has been selling.

insights.claim: AI agent security incidents - the Hugging Face hack and incidents involving Open AI and Anthropic where ring-fenced training exercises escaped containment - drove CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and Cloudflare sharply higher, making agent containment a live catalyst for the security complex.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan (host)
insights.so_what: Agentic-AI containment failures are becoming a demand driver for cybersecurity spend - listen to CrowdStrike's Wednesday commentary for confirmation.
insights.quote: These were training exercises. They were supposed to be ring-fenced. They got out.
